topics.name: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
topics.summary: Electric potential at a point is the work done by an external agent per unit positive test charge in bringing it slowly from infinity to that point, so its unit is the volt (\( \text{J C}^{-1} \)). For a point charge, \( V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r} \): positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative one, and falling as \( 1/r \). The most important fact is that potential is a signed scalar. For a system of charges you simply add the individual potentials algebraically, \( V=\sum\dfrac{kq_i}{r_i} \), keeping each sign and ignoring directions completely. There are no components and no angles as there would be for the field. So the potential can be zero where the field is not (midpoint of \( +q \) and \( -q \)), and nonzero where the field is zero (midpoint of two equal like charges). For a short dipole, the far-field potential is \( V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2} \): maximum on the axis, zero everywhere on the equatorial line, negative on the side of the negative charge, and falling as \( 1/r^2 \).
topics.worked_example: Charges \( +4\ \text{nC} \) and \( +3\ \text{nC} \) are each \( 0.3\ \text{m} \) from P, along perpendicular lines. \( V_P=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-9}}{0.3}+\dfrac{9\times10^9\times3\times10^{-9}}{0.3}=120+90=210\ \text{V} \). The right angle is irrelevant: potentials add as plain numbers.
common_mistakes: Combining potentials like vectors, with components or \( \sqrt{V_1^2+V_2^2} \), instead of adding them algebraically.
Dropping the negative sign of the potential due to a negative charge.
Using \( 1/r^2 \) (field law) instead of \( 1/r \) for a point charge, or \( 1/r \) instead of \( 1/r^2 \) for a dipole.
Assuming zero field means zero potential, or zero potential means zero field.

topics.name: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
topics.summary: An equipotential surface is a surface on which the potential has the same value everywhere. For a point charge these are concentric spheres; for a uniform field they are parallel planes perpendicular to the field. The field is always perpendicular to equipotentials, and where the field is stronger, surfaces with equal steps of potential crowd closer together. Two equipotentials never intersect. The field and potential are linked by \( E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr} \): the magnitude of E is the rate of change of V, and the minus sign means E points in the direction of decreasing potential. In a uniform field, \( V=Ed \) along the field. The work done by an external agent moving a charge q slowly from A to B is \( W=q(V_B-V_A) \), final minus initial, and it depends only on the end points, never on the path. Along an equipotential, or between two points on the same equipotential, this work is exactly zero. A free positive charge moves towards lower potential; a free negative charge moves towards higher potential.
key_formulas: Uniform field: \( V=Ed \) (d along the field)
topics.worked_example: A \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) charge is moved from A (\( 10\ \text{V} \)) to B (\( 50\ \text{V} \)). \( W=q(V_B-V_A)=2\times10^{-6}\times(50-10)=8\times10^{-5}\ \text{J} \). If B were on the same equipotential as A, the work would be zero for any path.
common_mistakes: Taking the field to point from low to high potential; it points towards decreasing potential.
Computing \( q(V_A-V_B) \) instead of \( q(V_B-V_A) \) for the external agent's work.
Claiming nonzero work for motion along an equipotential, or thinking the work depends on the path.
Forgetting the minus sign in \( E=-dV/dx \), or using the full distance instead of its component along the field.

topics.name: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
topics.summary: The potential energy of two point charges is \( U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} \): positive for like charges, negative for unlike charges. For a system of several charges, add one such term for every distinct pair: three charges give three pair terms (12, 13, 23), not three single-charge terms and not six. A charge q placed where external charges produce potential V has energy \( U=qV \), and a dipole in a uniform field has \( U=-pE\cos\theta \). Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium have zero field inside; any excess charge lies on the outer surface; the whole conductor, surface included, is one equipotential, so field lines meet the surface at right angles; and the field just outside is \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \), normal to the surface. A charged conducting sphere has potential \( kQ/R \) everywhere inside, not zero. An empty cavity inside a conductor is shielded from outside fields. Connected conductors reach a common potential, so charge divides in proportion to radius and density is highest at sharp points.
topics.worked_example: Three charges of \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side \( 0.1\ \text{m} \). There are 3 pairs, each with \( U=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times10^{-12}}{0.1}=0.09\ \text{J} \), so \( U_{\text{total}}=0.27\ \text{J} \).
common_mistakes: Counting only some pairs, or counting every pair twice.
Ignoring the signs of the charges in the pair products.
Assuming zero field inside a conductor means zero potential there.
Using \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) for the field just outside a conductor instead of \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \).

topics.name: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
topics.summary: A capacitor stores charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance \( C=Q/V \), in farad, depends only on geometry and the medium, never on Q or V separately. For a parallel plate capacitor \( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d} \), and between the plates \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0=V/d \). Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant K always increases the capacitance to \( C=KC_0 \), because polarisation charges reduce the field. What happens next depends on the invariant. If the capacitor is isolated (disconnected), Q stays fixed, so V and E fall by a factor K. If it stays connected to a battery, V stays fixed, so Q rises by K and E is unchanged. The same logic applies when the plate separation changes. A slab of thickness t fills only part of the gap: \( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d-t+t/K} \), and a metal slab (K effectively infinite) simply removes t from the gap. Side-by-side dielectrics act in parallel; stacked layers act in series.
key_formulas: Isolated: \( Q \) fixed, \( V=\dfrac{V_0}{K} \); connected: \( V \) fixed, \( Q=KQ_0 \)
topics.worked_example: A \( 5\ \text{pF} \) capacitor is charged to \( 12\ \text{V} \) (Q = 60 pC) and disconnected, then filled with K = 4. C becomes 20 pF with Q still 60 pC, so \( V=60/20=3\ \text{V} \). Had it stayed connected, V would stay 12 V and Q would become 240 pC.
common_mistakes: Treating Q as fixed while the battery is still connected, or V as fixed after it has been disconnected.
Thinking capacitance depends on the charge or the voltage.
Multiplying by K when only part of the gap is filled.
Dividing the field by K even when the battery keeps the voltage fixed.

topics.name: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
topics.summary: Capacitor combination rules are the reverse of resistor rules. In series, \( \dfrac{1}{C_{eq}}=\sum\dfrac{1}{C_i} \), so the result is smaller than the smallest capacitor. Every capacitor carries the same charge, and the voltage divides as \( V_i=Q/C_i \), with the smallest capacitor taking the largest voltage. In parallel, \( C_{eq}=\sum C_i \), larger than any one. Every capacitor has the same voltage, and the charge divides as \( Q_i=C_iV \). The energy stored is \( U=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac12QV \), held in the field with energy density \( u=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \). A battery does work QV while charging, but only half is stored. When two capacitors charged to different voltages are connected, total charge is conserved and the common potential is \( \dfrac{Q_1+Q_2}{C_1+C_2} \). Stored energy, however, always decreases unless they started at the same potential. Inserting a dielectric lowers the energy of an isolated capacitor (\( U_0/K \)) but raises that of a connected one (\( KU_0 \)).
topics.worked_example: \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) in series across \( 90\ \text{V} \): \( C_{eq}=2\ \mu\text{F} \), \( Q=180\ \mu\text{C} \) on each. \( V_3=60\ \text{V} \), \( V_6=30\ \text{V} \); energy in the \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) is \( \tfrac12\times6\times10^{-6}\times30^2=2.7\times10^{-3}\ \text{J} \).
common_mistakes: Using resistor formulas for capacitors: adding in series or adding reciprocals in parallel.
Swapping the common quantity: series capacitors share charge, parallel capacitors share voltage.
Assuming energy is conserved when charged capacitors are connected together; only charge is conserved.
Dropping the factor \( \tfrac12 \) in the energy formulas.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Electric potential at a point is best described as which kind of quantity?
options: A scalar, which can be positive or negative
A vector directed along the electric field
A vector directed opposite to the electric field
A scalar that is always positive
questions.explanation:
Potential is work done per unit charge, \( V=W/q_0 \), and work is a scalar, so potential has no direction.

Its sign follows the source: potential is positive near a positive charge and negative near a negative charge.
questions.hint: Recall how potential is defined: work per unit charge. Does work have a direction?
distractor_logic: Treats potential like the electric field; potential is a scalar and has no direction.
Also treats potential as a vector; the minus sign in \( E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr} \) links the field to the potential gradient, it does not give V a direction.
Forgets that a negative source charge produces a negative potential.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: The SI unit of electric potential, the volt, is equivalent to
questions.explanation:
Potential is work per unit charge: \( V=\dfrac{W}{q} \).

So \( 1\ \text{V}=1\ \text{J}/1\ \text{C}=1\ \text{J C}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Potential = energy divided by charge.
distractor_logic: \( \text{N C}^{-1} \) is the unit of electric field, not potential.
Multiplies energy by charge instead of dividing.
Inverts the ratio: charge per unit energy.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: The electric potential at a distance \( r \) from a point charge \( q \) is
questions.explanation:
Bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to distance \( r \) against the field of \( q \) requires work \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r} \).

So potential falls off as \( 1/r \), not \( 1/r^2 \).
questions.hint: Potential falls off more slowly than the field does.
distractor_logic: This is the field magnitude \( E \), which goes as \( 1/r^2 \); potential goes as \( 1/r \).
Squares the charge; potential is linear in the source charge.
Makes potential grow with distance; it must fall to zero at infinity.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A point charge \( q=+2\ \text{nC} \) is fixed in air. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The electric potential at a point \( 30\ \text{cm} \) from it is
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{kq}{r}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-9}}{0.30} \)

\( V=\dfrac{18}{0.30}=60\ \text{V} \), positive because the charge is positive.
questions.hint: Use \( V=kq/r \) with \( r \) in metres.
distractor_logic: Divides by \( r^2 \), which gives the field in V/m, not the potential.
Stops at \( kq=18 \) and forgets to divide by \( r \).
Gives a negative sign even though the source charge is positive.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A point charge \( q=-3\ \text{nC} \) is fixed in air. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at a point \( 30\ \text{cm} \) from it is
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{kq}{r}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times(-3\times10^{-9})}{0.30} \)

\( V=\dfrac{-27}{0.30}=-90\ \text{V} \). The sign of the charge is carried into the potential.
questions.hint: Keep the sign of the charge inside the formula.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; potential due to a negative charge is negative.
Divides by \( r^2 \) instead of \( r \).
Forgets to divide by \( r \).

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: The electric potential at a point is defined as the
options: force experienced by a unit positive charge placed at that point
work done by an external agent per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point without acceleration
work done by an external agent in bringing any charge, of whatever size, from infinity to that point
work done per unit charge in moving a test charge from that point to the source charge
questions.explanation:
Potential is work per unit positive test charge, measured from the reference point at infinity where V = 0.

The charge is moved slowly (no acceleration) so that all the work goes into potential energy.
questions.hint: Two keys: per unit charge, and starting from infinity.
distractor_logic: That is the definition of electric field, not potential.
Leaves out 'per unit charge'; that describes potential energy, not potential.
Uses the wrong reference point; potential is measured relative to infinity.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Charges \( +q \) and \( -q \) are separated by a distance \( d \). The electric potential at the midpoint of the line joining them is
questions.explanation:
Each charge is \( d/2 \) away, so the contributions are \( +\dfrac{kq}{d/2} \) and \( -\dfrac{kq}{d/2} \).

Potential is a signed scalar, so they add algebraically to zero (even though the field there is not zero).
questions.hint: Add the two contributions with their signs.
distractor_logic: Adds magnitudes and ignores the negative sign of one charge.
This is the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint, not the potential.
Counts only one of the two charges.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Far from a short electric dipole (\( r\gg a \)), the potential at a point on its axis varies with distance \( r \) as
questions.explanation:
For a dipole, \( V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2} \).

The \( +q \) and \( -q \) contributions nearly cancel, leaving a \( 1/r^2 \) fall-off, faster than a single charge's \( 1/r \).
questions.hint: The two opposite charges almost cancel each other far away.
distractor_logic: That is the fall-off for a single point charge, not a dipole.
That is how the dipole's field falls off, not its potential.
Potential of any finite charge system must fall off with distance.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are
options: concentric spheres centred on the charge
coaxial cylinders around a line through the charge
straight lines radiating out from the charge
questions.explanation: \( V=kq/r \) depends only on \( r \), so every surface of constant \( r \), a sphere centred on the charge, is an equipotential.
questions.hint: Which points have the same distance r from the charge?
distractor_logic: Planes are the equipotentials of a uniform field, not a point charge.
Cylinders are the equipotentials of a long line charge.
Radial lines are the field lines, which are perpendicular to the equipotentials.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: In a uniform electric field, the equipotential surfaces are
options: planes parallel to the field lines
planes perpendicular to the field lines
planes inclined at 45 degrees to the field lines
questions.explanation:
Potential changes only along the field: \( \Delta V=-E\,\Delta x \).

Moving perpendicular to the field keeps V constant, so equipotentials are planes perpendicular to E.
questions.hint: Along which direction does the potential not change at all?
distractor_logic: Moving along the field changes V, so planes containing the field cannot be equipotentials.
Spheres are the equipotentials of a point charge.
The field is always perpendicular to equipotentials, never at 45 degrees.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: At any point, the electric field is directed
options: parallel (tangent) to the equipotential surface through that point
at an angle that depends on the charge distribution
perpendicular to the equipotential surface through that point
along the equipotential surface, towards higher potential
questions.explanation:
If the field had a component along an equipotential surface, moving a charge along the surface would need work, contradicting V = constant.

So E has no tangential component: it is normal to the surface.
questions.hint: Think about the work done moving along an equipotential.
distractor_logic: A tangential field would do work along the surface, so V would not be constant there.
The perpendicular relation holds for every charge distribution.
Combines the tangent error with a direction error; the field points towards lower potential.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A charge \( q \) is moved between two points on the same equipotential surface. The work done is
options: \( qV \), where \( V \) is the potential of the surface
zero only if the path stays on the surface
positive or negative depending on the sign of q
questions.explanation:
\( W=q(V_B-V_A) \), and on an equipotential \( V_B=V_A \).

Since electrostatic work depends only on the end points, W = 0 for any path joining them.
questions.hint: Use \( W=q(V_B-V_A) \).
distractor_logic: Uses the potential itself instead of the potential difference.
Electrostatic work is path-independent; only the end points matter.
The sign of q cannot matter when \( V_B-V_A=0 \).

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: The electric field always points in the direction in which the electric potential
questions.explanation: \( E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr} \): the minus sign means E points towards decreasing potential, and the steepest decrease gives its magnitude.
questions.hint: Look at the minus sign in \( E=-dV/dr \).
distractor_logic: Reverses the direction; the field points from high to low potential.
Along the directions of constant potential, the field has no component.
Along a field line, potential changes monotonically.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: The unit volt per metre is equivalent to
questions.explanation:
\( 1\ \text{V m}^{-1}=1\ \text{J C}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}=1\ \text{N m}\,\text{C}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}=1\ \text{N C}^{-1} \).

So field can be expressed either as potential gradient or as force per unit charge.
questions.hint: Write the joule as newton times metre.
distractor_logic: \( \text{J C}^{-1} \) is the volt itself; the 'per metre' is missing.
Forgets to divide by the metre.
Inverts the ratio.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Two different equipotential surfaces can never intersect because
options: the field is zero wherever two surfaces meet
equipotential surfaces are always parallel planes
the point of intersection would have two different potentials
charge cannot exist on an equipotential surface
questions.explanation:
Each equipotential has a single value of V. A common point would need two values of V at once, which is impossible.

It would also need two different field directions (one normal to each surface).
questions.hint: Potential at a point has only one value.
distractor_logic: There is no such rule; the real reason is the single-valued potential.
Equipotentials are planes only for a uniform field.
Charges can sit on equipotentials; a conductor surface is one.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: In a region where the electric field is strong, equally spaced values of potential (for example 10 V, 20 V, 30 V) correspond to equipotential surfaces that are
questions.explanation: \( |E|=\dfrac{|\Delta V|}{\Delta r} \), so for a fixed \( \Delta V \), a larger E means a smaller gap \( \Delta r \).
questions.hint: Field = change in V per unit distance.
distractor_logic: Reverses the relation; strong fields crowd the surfaces together.
Equal spacing happens only in a uniform field.
The spacing is set directly by the field strength.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: The electrostatic potential energy of two point charges \( q_1 \) and \( q_2 \) separated by distance \( r \) is
questions.explanation:
Bring \( q_1 \) in first (no work). Then bring \( q_2 \) to distance \( r \): work \( =q_2V_1=q_2\cdot\dfrac{kq_1}{r} \).

So \( U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} \), a product of charges over the first power of r.
questions.hint: Energy = charge times potential.
distractor_logic: That is the Coulomb force, which goes as \( 1/r^2 \).
Energy involves the product of the charges, not their sum.
Energy must fall towards zero as the charges separate.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Two positive point charges are pushed closer together. Their mutual electrostatic potential energy
questions.explanation:
\( U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} \) is positive for like charges and grows as r shrinks.

Work must be done against the repulsion, and it is stored as potential energy.
questions.hint: Like charges repel; you must push to bring them together.
distractor_logic: That is what happens for unlike charges, which attract.
U depends on r, so it must change.
U becomes zero only at infinite separation.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is
options: equal to the field just outside the surface
questions.explanation: If there were a field inside, the free electrons would move. In equilibrium they have stopped moving, so the net field inside is zero.
questions.hint: What would free electrons do if a field existed inside?
distractor_logic: Any nonzero field would keep driving a current, contradicting equilibrium.
There is no field at all inside, at the centre or elsewhere.
The field just outside is \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \); inside it is zero.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Any excess charge given to an isolated conductor resides
options: partly inside and partly on the surface in equal amounts
questions.explanation:
Since E = 0 inside, Gauss's law applied to any surface just inside the conductor encloses zero charge.

So the excess charge must sit on the outer surface.
questions.hint: Apply Gauss's law to a surface just inside the conductor.
distractor_logic: Volume charge would create a field inside, which cannot exist in equilibrium.
Charge at the centre would produce a field inside the conductor.
No excess charge can remain in the interior.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: In electrostatic equilibrium, the surface of a conductor is
options: a surface along which the field is tangential
a surface where potential is highest at sharp points
questions.explanation:
The field has no tangential component at the surface (otherwise charges would move along it), so no work is done moving along the surface.

Hence the whole surface, and indeed the whole conductor, is at one potential.
questions.hint: No work is done moving a charge along the surface.
distractor_logic: The field at the surface is normal, not tangential.
The potential is constant, but not necessarily zero.
Charge density may be higher at sharp points, but the potential is the same everywhere.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Just outside the surface of a charged conductor with local surface charge density \( \sigma \), the electric field is
questions.explanation:
A small Gaussian pill-box with one face inside (E = 0) and one just outside gives \( EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0} \).

So \( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} \), directed normal to the surface.
questions.hint: Only one face of the pill-box has field through it.
distractor_logic: \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) is for an isolated thin sheet with field on both sides.
The field at a conductor surface has no tangential part.
The field is zero inside the conductor, not just outside it.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A hollow conductor has an empty cavity inside. When the conductor is placed in an external electric field, the field inside the cavity is
options: directed opposite to the external field
questions.explanation:
Charges rearrange on the outer surface so that the field in the conductor, and in any empty cavity within it, is zero.

This is electrostatic shielding.
questions.hint: Think of electrostatic shielding.
distractor_logic: The conductor shields the cavity completely.
There is no partial shielding in electrostatics.
The induced charges cancel the field; they do not reverse it.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Charges \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( +3\ \mu\text{C} \) are \( 30\ \text{cm} \) apart. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). Their electrostatic potential energy is
questions.explanation:
\( U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-6}\times3\times10^{-6}}{0.3} \).

\( U=\dfrac{0.054}{0.3}=0.18\ \text{J} \), positive for like charges.
distractor_logic: Like charges have positive potential energy.
Forgets to divide by r.
Divides by \( r^2 \), as in Coulomb's law.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: The capacitance of a capacitor is defined as
questions.explanation:
Capacitance is charge stored per unit potential difference: \( C=Q/V \).

Its unit is \( 1\ \text{F}=1\ \text{C V}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Charge stored per volt.
distractor_logic: Multiplies instead of dividing.
Inverts the ratio.
The volt is the unit of potential, not capacitance.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with plate area \( A \) and separation \( d \) in vacuum is
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{Q}{\epsilon_0A} \) and \( V=Ed=\dfrac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A} \).

\( C=\dfrac{Q}{V}=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d} \).
questions.hint: Bigger plates store more; wider gaps store less.
distractor_logic: Inverts area and separation.
Puts \( \epsilon_0 \) in the denominator.
Capacitance must decrease as d grows.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor of capacitance \( C_0 \) (vacuum between plates) is completely filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant \( K \). Its new capacitance is
questions.explanation:
The dielectric reduces the field for a given charge by a factor K, so V falls by K for the same Q.

\( C=\dfrac{Q}{V}=KC_0 \).
questions.hint: A dielectric always increases capacitance.
distractor_logic: A dielectric increases capacitance; it does not reduce it.
The capacitance depends on the medium between the plates.
The factor is K, not its square.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor depends on
options: the potential difference applied across it
both the charge on the plates and the applied voltage
the plate area, the plate separation and the medium between the plates
questions.explanation:
\( C=\dfrac{K\epsilon_0A}{d} \) contains only geometry and the medium.

If Q doubles, V doubles too, and \( Q/V \) stays the same.
questions.hint: Look at what appears in the capacitance formula.
distractor_logic: Changing Q changes V in proportion; C is unaffected.
Changing V changes Q in proportion; C is unaffected.
Neither Q nor V appears in the formula for C.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor holds a charge of \( 6\ \mu\text{C} \) when the potential difference across it is \( 3\ \text{V} \). Its capacitance is
questions.explanation: \( C=\dfrac{Q}{V}=\dfrac{6\ \mu\text{C}}{3\ \text{V}}=2\ \mu\text{F} \).
distractor_logic: Multiplies Q by V.
Divides V by Q.
Adds a stray factor of one half, as in the energy formula.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: If the separation between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled (nothing else changed), its capacitance
questions.explanation: \( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d}\propto\dfrac1d \), so doubling d halves C.
questions.hint: C varies inversely with d.
distractor_logic: Treats C as proportional to d.
C depends on the geometry, including d.
C goes as \( 1/d \), not \( 1/d^2 \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor carrying a fixed charge has a field \( E_0 \) between its plates. When the gap is filled with a dielectric of constant \( K \), the field becomes
questions.explanation:
The dielectric polarises, and its induced surface charges oppose the applied field.

With the free charge fixed, the net field is reduced to \( E_0/K \).
questions.hint: Polarisation charges partly cancel the field.
distractor_logic: The induced charges oppose the field, so it cannot grow.
The dielectric does change the field when the charge is fixed.
A dielectric reduces the field but, unlike a conductor, does not cancel it.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area \( 0.02\ \text{m}^2 \) separated by \( 1\ \text{mm} \) of air. Take \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2} \). Its capacitance is
questions.explanation:
\( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d}=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.02}{1\times10^{-3}} \).

\( C=1.77\times10^{-10}\ \text{F}=177\ \text{pF} \).
questions.hint: Convert mm to m.
distractor_logic: Takes d as 1 m, not 1 mm.
Introduces a stray factor of 2.
Introduces a stray factor of one half.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: For capacitors \( C_1,C_2,\ldots \) connected in series, the equivalent capacitance satisfies
questions.explanation:
In series each capacitor has the same Q, and the voltages add: \( V=\dfrac{Q}{C_1}+\dfrac{Q}{C_2}+\ldots \).

Dividing by Q: \( \dfrac1{C_{eq}}=\sum\dfrac1{C_i} \). This is the form of resistors in parallel.
questions.hint: Same charge, voltages add.
distractor_logic: This is the parallel rule for capacitors (or series rule for resistors).
The product-over-sum shortcut is valid only for exactly two capacitors.
No such geometric-mean rule exists.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: For capacitors \( C_1,C_2,\ldots \) connected in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation:
In parallel each capacitor has the same V, and the charges add: \( Q=C_1V+C_2V+\ldots \).

So \( C_{eq}=\sum C_i \), like resistors in series.
questions.hint: Same voltage, charges add.
distractor_logic: This is the series rule for capacitors, borrowed from resistors in parallel.
Averaging would make the combination no better than one capacitor.
The combination stores more than any single capacitor.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: When capacitors are connected in series across a battery, the quantity that is the same for every capacitor is the
questions.explanation:
Charge moves onto the outer plates and induces equal and opposite charges on each inner plate pair, so every capacitor carries the same Q.

The voltage then divides as V = Q/C.
questions.hint: Think about induction between neighbouring plates.
distractor_logic: Common voltage is the property of a parallel connection.
Energy Q squared over 2C differs when C differs.
The capacitors may have any capacitances.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: When capacitors are connected in parallel across a battery, the quantity that is the same for every capacitor is the
questions.explanation:
Each capacitor is connected directly between the same two points, so each has the full battery voltage.

The charge then divides as Q = CV.
questions.hint: Each capacitor sits across the same two terminals.
distractor_logic: Common charge is the property of a series connection.
Energy one half C V squared differs when C differs.
The field V/d differs if the plate separations differ.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A capacitor of capacitance \( C \) has charge \( Q \) and potential difference \( V \). The energy stored in it is
questions.explanation: Charging from 0 to Q against a rising voltage: \( U=\displaystyle\int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac12QV \).
questions.hint: The average voltage during charging is half the final voltage.
distractor_logic: Misses the factor one half.
V must be squared for units of energy.
Misses the factor one half in the charge form.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Two capacitors of \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) each are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation: \( \dfrac1{C_{eq}}=\dfrac16+\dfrac16=\dfrac13 \), so \( C_{eq}=3\ \mu\text{F} \), smaller than either.
questions.hint: Series capacitance is less than the smallest one.
distractor_logic: Adds them, which is the parallel rule.
Assumes identical capacitors in series change nothing.
Multiplies the capacitances.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 10\ \text{V} \). The energy stored is
questions.explanation: \( U=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac12\times4\times10^{-6}\times100=2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: \( U=\tfrac12CV^2 \).
distractor_logic: Forgets the factor one half.
Forgets to square V.
Uses one quarter instead of one half.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: The energy stored per unit volume in an electric field \( E \) in vacuum is
questions.explanation:
For a parallel plate capacitor, \( U=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac12\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d}(Ed)^2=\dfrac12\epsilon_0E^2(Ad) \).

Dividing by the volume Ad gives \( u=\dfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \).
questions.hint: Divide the capacitor's energy by its volume.
distractor_logic: Misses the factor one half.
E must be squared.
Puts \( \epsilon_0 \) in the denominator.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Charges \( +4\ \text{nC} \) and \( +3\ \text{nC} \) are fixed at points A and B. Point P is \( 30\ \text{cm} \) from each of them, with \( \angle APB=90^\circ \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at P is
questions.explanation:
\( V_A=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-9}}{0.30}=120\ \text{V} \) and \( V_B=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times3\times10^{-9}}{0.30}=90\ \text{V} \).

Potential is a scalar, so \( V_P=120+90=210\ \text{V} \). The \( 90^\circ \) angle plays no role.
questions.hint: The angle between AP and BP is a distraction for potential.
distractor_logic: Combines the two potentials like perpendicular vectors, \( \sqrt{120^2+90^2} \); potential is not a vector.
Subtracts the contributions although both charges are positive.
Combines the field magnitudes \( kq/r^2 \) (400 and 300) as vectors; that is a field calculation, not potential.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A charge \( +5\ \text{nC} \) is at \( x=0 \) and a charge \( -3\ \text{nC} \) is at \( x=0.6\ \text{m} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at \( x=0.3\ \text{m} \) is
questions.explanation:
Both charges are \( 0.3\ \text{m} \) away: \( V=\dfrac{9\times10^9}{0.3}\left(5\times10^{-9}-3\times10^{-9}\right) \).

\( V=150-90=60\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Keep the sign of each charge and add.
distractor_logic: Adds 150 V and 90 V, ignoring that the second charge is negative.
Reverses the signs of both contributions.
Assumes the midpoint of any two opposite charges is at zero potential; that holds only for equal magnitudes.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A charge \( +1\ \text{nC} \) is at \( x=0 \) and \( -3\ \text{nC} \) is at \( x=1.2\ \text{m} \). At which point between them is the electric potential zero?
questions.explanation:
Set \( \dfrac{k(1)}{x}+\dfrac{k(-3)}{1.2-x}=0 \Rightarrow 1.2-x=3x \).

\( x=0.3\ \text{m} \), closer to the smaller charge, as expected.
questions.hint: The zero-potential point lies closer to the smaller-magnitude charge.
distractor_logic: Swaps the roles of the charges, placing the point near the larger charge.
Assumes V = 0 at the midpoint, which needs equal magnitudes.
Divides the separation by the charge ratio, 1.2/3, instead of splitting it in the ratio 1 : 3.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A short dipole has dipole moment \( p=4\times10^{-9}\ \text{C m} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at an axial point \( 0.6\ \text{m} \) from its centre (\( r\gg a \)) is
questions.explanation:
On the axis, \( V=\dfrac{kp}{r^2}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-9}}{0.36} \).

\( V=\dfrac{36}{0.36}=100\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Dipole potential on the axis: \( kp/r^2 \).
distractor_logic: Divides by \( r \) instead of \( r^2 \), as for a point charge.
Borrows the factor 2 from the axial field formula \( 2kp/r^3 \).
Zero is the potential on the equatorial line, not the axis.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A short dipole of moment \( p=2\times10^{-9}\ \text{C m} \) is at the origin. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at a point \( 0.3\ \text{m} \) away, on a line making \( 60^\circ \) with the dipole axis, is
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-9}\times\cos60^\circ}{0.09} \).

\( V=200\times\dfrac12=100\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: The general formula uses \( \cos\theta \), where \( \theta \) is measured from the axis.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \sin\theta \) instead of \( \cos\theta \).
Ignores the \( \cos\theta \) factor altogether.
Uses \( \cos^2\theta \) instead of \( \cos\theta \).

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A short dipole of moment \( p=2\times10^{-9}\ \text{C m} \) lies along the x-axis. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at a point on its equatorial line, \( 0.5\ \text{m} \) from its centre, is
questions.explanation:
Every equatorial point is equidistant from \( +q \) and \( -q \), so \( \dfrac{kq}{r'}-\dfrac{kq}{r'}=0 \).

Equivalently \( \theta=90^\circ \) gives \( \cos\theta=0 \) in \( V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2} \).
questions.hint: On the equatorial line both charges are at the same distance.
distractor_logic: Uses the axial value \( kp/r^2 \) at an equatorial point.
Takes half the axial value, borrowing the equatorial field's ratio to the axial field.
Doubles the axial value, mixing up potential with the axial field formula.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Charges \( +2\ \text{nC} \), \( +2\ \text{nC} \) and \( -1\ \text{nC} \) sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Each vertex is \( 10\ \text{cm} \) from the centroid. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at the centroid is
questions.explanation:
All three charges are \( 0.1\ \text{m} \) from the centroid: \( V=\dfrac{k}{0.1}(2+2-1)\times10^{-9} \).

\( V=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times3\times10^{-9}}{0.1}=270\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Same distance for every charge, so just add the signed charges.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes 2 + 2 + 1, ignoring the negative sign.
Assumes a symmetric arrangement gives zero potential; that is true of the field in some cases, never automatically of V.
Leaves out the negative charge entirely.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A point charge \( +5\ \text{nC} \) is fixed. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work needed to bring a charge \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) slowly from infinity to a point \( 45\ \text{cm} \) from it is
questions.explanation:
Potential at the point: \( V=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times5\times10^{-9}}{0.45}=100\ \text{V} \).

Work \( W=qV=2\times10^{-6}\times100=2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \), positive because like charges repel.
questions.hint: First find V at the point, then use \( W=qV \).
distractor_logic: Wrong sign: pushing a positive charge towards a positive charge needs positive external work.
Uses \( 1\ \mu\text{C}=10^{-4}\ \text{C} \) instead of \( 10^{-6}\ \text{C} \).
Introduces a spurious factor of one half.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Two large parallel plates are \( 5\ \text{cm} \) apart with a potential difference of \( 100\ \text{V} \) between them. The magnitude of the uniform field between them is
questions.hint: Convert cm to m before dividing.
distractor_logic: Divides by 5 without converting cm to m.
Multiplies V by d in metres instead of dividing.
Multiplies V by d in centimetres.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Point A is at potential \( 10\ \text{V} \) and point B is at \( 50\ \text{V} \). The work done by an external agent in slowly moving a charge \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) from A to B is
questions.explanation:
\( W=q(V_B-V_A)=2\times10^{-6}\times(50-10) \).

\( W=8\times10^{-5}\ \text{J} \), positive: the positive charge is pushed to higher potential.
questions.hint: Final minus initial: \( V_B-V_A \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( V_A-V_B \), the wrong order.
Adds the two potentials instead of subtracting.
Uses only \( qV_B \), ignoring the starting potential.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A charge \( -3\ \mu\text{C} \) is moved slowly from point A (\( V_A=20\ \text{V} \)) to point B (\( V_B=-10\ \text{V} \)). The work done by the external agent is
questions.explanation:
\( W=q(V_B-V_A)=(-3\times10^{-6})\times(-10-20) \).

\( W=(-3\times10^{-6})\times(-30)=+9\times10^{-5}\ \text{J} \): a negative charge is being pushed to lower potential, against its natural tendency.
questions.hint: Carry both signs: the charge's and the potential difference's.
distractor_logic: Uses \( V_A-V_B \), flipping the sign.
Uses only \( qV_B \), ignoring \( V_A \).
Adds \( V_A \) and \( V_B \) instead of subtracting.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: The potential along the x-axis is \( V(x)=5x^2-3x \) (V in volts, x in metres). The x-component of the electric field at \( x=1\ \text{m} \) is
questions.hint: Differentiate, then remember the minus sign.
distractor_logic: Forgets the minus sign in \( E=-dV/dx \).
Uses the value of \( -V(1) \) rather than the derivative.
Differentiates only \( 5x^2 \) and drops the \( -3x \) term.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A uniform field of \( 200\ \text{V m}^{-1} \) points along \( +x \). The potential at \( x=0 \) is \( 50\ \text{V} \). The potential at \( x=0.2\ \text{m} \) is
questions.explanation:
Moving along the field, potential falls: \( \Delta V=-E\,\Delta x=-200\times0.2=-40\ \text{V} \).

\( V=50-40=10\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Potential decreases in the direction of the field.
distractor_logic: Adds the drop instead of subtracting; potential falls along the field.
Assumes potential stays constant in a uniform field.
Reports the size of the change instead of the new potential.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Three parallel equipotential planes are at \( 10\ \text{V} \), \( 20\ \text{V} \) and \( 30\ \text{V} \), with adjacent planes \( 0.5\ \text{cm} \) apart. The electric field in this region is
options: \( 2000\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), directed from the 10 V plane towards the 30 V plane
\( 2000\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), directed from the 30 V plane towards the 10 V plane
\( 20\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), directed from the 30 V plane towards the 10 V plane
\( 6000\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), directed from the 30 V plane towards the 10 V plane
questions.explanation:
\( |E|=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}=\dfrac{10}{0.005}=2000\ \text{V m}^{-1} \).

The field points towards decreasing potential: from 30 V towards 10 V, perpendicular to the planes.
questions.hint: Magnitude from the gradient; direction towards lower V.
distractor_logic: Right magnitude, but the field points from low to high potential here; it must point towards lower V.
Divides by 0.5 without converting cm to m.
Uses the total 20 V difference across only one 0.5 cm gap.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A charge \( +5\ \mu\text{C} \) is carried halfway around a circle of radius \( 20\ \text{cm} \) centred on a fixed point charge \( +10\ \text{nC} \). The work done by the external agent is
questions.explanation:
The circle is centred on the point charge, so every point on it has the same potential; it lies on an equipotential sphere.

\( W=q(V_B-V_A)=0 \).
questions.hint: Is the distance from the fixed charge changing along the path?
distractor_logic: This is \( qV \) at the circle, the work to bring the charge in from infinity, not to move it along the circle.
Same as \( qV \) but with the wrong sign.
Doubles \( qV \), as if work accumulates along the arc.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A uniform field \( E=500\ \text{V m}^{-1} \) points along \( +x \). Point A is at \( (0,0) \) and B at \( (0.4\ \text{m},\,0.3\ \text{m}) \). The potential difference \( V_A-V_B \) is
questions.explanation:
Only displacement along the field changes V: \( V_A-V_B=E(x_B-x_A)=500\times0.4 \).

\( V_A-V_B=200\ \text{V} \); A is at the higher potential because B lies further along the field.
questions.hint: Only the component of displacement along the field matters.
distractor_logic: Uses the full distance AB = 0.5 m instead of its component along the field.
Uses the y-displacement, which is perpendicular to the field.
Gets the sign wrong; potential falls along the field, so A is higher.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Three charges, each \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \), are at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side \( 10\ \text{cm} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The total electrostatic potential energy of the system is
questions.explanation:
Count every pair once: 3 charges give 3 pairs (12, 23, 13).

Each pair: \( \dfrac{9\times10^9\times10^{-12}}{0.1}=0.09\ \text{J} \).

\( U=3\times0.09=0.27\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: List the distinct pairs of charges.
distractor_logic: Counts only one pair.
Counts each pair twice (6 ordered pairs instead of 3).
Counts only two of the three pairs.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Charges \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \), \( -1\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) are placed at \( x=0 \), \( x=0.1\ \text{m} \) and \( x=0.2\ \text{m} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The electrostatic potential energy of the system is
questions.hint: Three pairs, including the two outer charges 0.2 m apart.
distractor_logic: Forgets the pair formed by the two outer charges.
Ignores the signs of the charges.
Counts just one neighbouring pair.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Two charges \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( +5\ \mu\text{C} \) are brought slowly from a separation of \( 30\ \text{cm} \) to \( 10\ \text{cm} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work done by the external agent is
questions.hint: Work by the agent = final PE minus initial PE.
distractor_logic: Wrong sign; pushing like charges together needs positive work.
Adds the initial and final energies.
Uses only the final energy, as if starting from infinity.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A solid conducting sphere of radius \( 10\ \text{cm} \) carries a charge \( 2\ \text{nC} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at its centre is
questions.explanation:
The whole conductor is an equipotential, so the centre has the surface potential \( \dfrac{kQ}{R} \).

\( V=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-9}}{0.1}=180\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Zero field inside means constant potential, not zero potential.
distractor_logic: Confuses zero field with zero potential.
Divides by \( R^2 \), giving the surface field in V/m.
Uses R/2 as if the centre were closer to the charge.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: The surface charge density at a point on a charged conductor is \( 8.85\times10^{-6}\ \text{C m}^{-2} \). Take \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2} \). The field just outside the conductor at that point is
questions.explanation: \( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-6}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=1\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Use \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0 \) at a conductor surface.
distractor_logic: Uses the thin-sheet result \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \).
Zero is the field inside, not outside.
Uses \( 2\sigma/\epsilon_0 \).

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A point charge \( +q \) is placed inside a cavity in an uncharged, isolated conductor. The charges that appear on the cavity wall and on the outer surface are
options: \( +q \) on the cavity wall and \( -q \) on the outer surface
\( -q \) on the cavity wall and \( +q \) on the outer surface
\( -q \) on the cavity wall and nothing on the outer surface
questions.explanation:
For E = 0 in the conductor, a Gaussian surface inside the metal must enclose zero net charge, so the cavity wall carries \( -q \).

The conductor is neutral overall, so \( +q \) appears on the outer surface.
questions.hint: Gauss's law inside the metal, plus overall neutrality.
distractor_logic: Signs reversed; the wall must cancel the enclosed +q.
Violates charge conservation; the uncharged conductor must stay neutral.
Then the field in the metal would not be zero.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: On an irregularly shaped charged conductor, the surface charge density is greatest
options: at the point farthest from the centre, whatever its shape
at the sharpest points, where the curvature is greatest
uniformly everywhere, since the surface is an equipotential
questions.explanation:
The surface is an equipotential. Regions of small radius of curvature need a larger charge density to hold the same potential.

So charge crowds at sharp points, where the field is also strongest.
questions.hint: Compare small and large spheres held at the same potential.
distractor_logic: Flat regions have the lowest density.
Density depends on curvature, not distance from the centre.
Equal potential does not mean equal charge density.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A charge \( -2\ \mu\text{C} \) is placed at a point where the potential due to external charges is \( 300\ \text{V} \). Its potential energy there is
questions.hint: \( U=qV \), keeping the sign of q.
distractor_logic: Drops the sign of the charge.
Divides V by q instead of multiplying.
Forgets the micro prefix.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor is charged to potential difference \( V_0 \) and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric slab of constant \( K=3 \) is now inserted to fill the gap. The new potential difference is
questions.explanation:
Disconnected: Q stays fixed. C becomes \( 3C_0 \).

\( V=\dfrac{Q}{3C_0}=\dfrac{V_0}{3} \).
questions.hint: Isolated capacitor: which quantity cannot change?
distractor_logic: Treats V as fixed, which is true only while the battery is connected.
Makes V rise, as if C decreased.
Divides by K twice.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor stays connected to a battery of voltage \( V \) while a dielectric slab of constant \( K \) is inserted to fill the gap. If its original charge was \( Q_0 \), the new charge is
questions.explanation:
Connected: V is held fixed by the battery. C becomes \( KC_0 \).

\( Q=KC_0V=KQ_0 \); the battery supplies the extra charge.
questions.hint: Connected capacitor: which quantity is fixed?
distractor_logic: Treats Q as fixed, which applies only to an isolated capacitor.
C increases, so Q at fixed V must increase too.
The factor is K, not its square.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A \( 5\ \text{pF} \) air capacitor is charged to \( 12\ \text{V} \), disconnected from the battery, and then completely filled with a dielectric of \( K=4 \). The new potential difference is
questions.explanation:
Q is fixed: \( Q=5\ \text{pF}\times12\ \text{V}=60\ \text{pC} \). New \( C=20\ \text{pF} \).

\( V=\dfrac{60}{20}=3\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Disconnected capacitor keeps its charge.
distractor_logic: Multiplies V by K instead of dividing.
Keeps V fixed as if still connected.
Divides by \( K^2 \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A \( 10\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor remains connected to a \( 6\ \text{V} \) battery while a dielectric of \( K=2 \) is inserted to fill the gap. The charge on the capacitor becomes
questions.explanation:
V stays 6 V. New \( C=20\ \mu\text{F} \).

\( Q=CV=20\times6=120\ \mu\text{C} \).
questions.hint: Battery connected: V is fixed.
distractor_logic: Keeps Q fixed as if disconnected.
Divides the charge by K.
Multiplies by \( K^2 \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor remains connected to a battery while its plate separation is doubled. If its original charge was \( Q \), the new charge is
questions.explanation:
C halves when d doubles, and V is fixed by the battery.

\( Q'=\dfrac{C}{2}V=\dfrac{Q}{2} \); charge flows back into the battery.
questions.hint: With the battery connected, V is the fixed quantity.
distractor_logic: Holds Q fixed, which applies only to an isolated capacitor.
C decreases, so the charge cannot increase.
C goes as \( 1/d \), not \( 1/d^2 \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor with plates \( 2\ \text{mm} \) apart is connected to a \( 100\ \text{V} \) battery. With the battery still connected, the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of \( K=5 \). The field in the dielectric is
questions.explanation:
The battery fixes V = 100 V across the same gap d = 2 mm.

\( E=\dfrac{V}{d}=\dfrac{100}{2\times10^{-3}}=5\times10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), the same as before; the extra charge drawn in exactly compensates the polarisation.
questions.hint: With V and d both fixed, \( E=V/d \) is fixed.
distractor_logic: Divides by K, which is correct only for an isolated (fixed-charge) capacitor.
Multiplies by K.
Leaves d in millimetres.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: The plates of an air capacitor carry surface charge densities \( \pm1.77\times10^{-6}\ \text{C m}^{-2} \) and are \( 1\ \text{mm} \) apart. Take \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2} \). The potential difference between the plates is
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{1.77\times10^{-6}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=2\times10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1} \).

\( V=Ed=2\times10^{5}\times10^{-3}=200\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Field between the plates is \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \); then multiply by d.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), the field of one plate alone.
Uses \( 2\sigma/\epsilon_0 \).
Stops at the field and forgets to multiply by d.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: Inserting a dielectric slab between the plates of a charged capacitor increases its capacitance mainly because
options: the dielectric adds extra free charge to the plates
the dielectric reduces the effective plate area
the dielectric conducts charge between the plates
the induced (polarisation) charges on the slab reduce the field, so a smaller voltage holds the same charge
questions.explanation:
The slab's bound surface charges oppose the plates' field, lowering E and hence V for a given Q.

Since \( C=Q/V \), a smaller V for the same Q means a larger C.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to V for a fixed Q.
distractor_logic: A dielectric has no free charge to add; only bound charges shift.
The plate area is unchanged; a smaller area would reduce C.
A dielectric is an insulator; conduction would discharge the capacitor.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Capacitors of \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \), \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac1{C_{eq}}=\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\dfrac16=\dfrac{3+2+1}{6}=1 \).

\( C_{eq}=1\ \mu\text{F} \), less than the smallest capacitor.
questions.hint: Add reciprocals.
distractor_logic: Adds directly, borrowing the resistor-series rule.
Assumes the combination equals the smallest capacitor; it is always smaller.
Picks the largest capacitor.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Capacitors of \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) are connected in series across a \( 90\ \text{V} \) supply. The potential difference across the \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is
questions.explanation:
\( C_{eq}=\dfrac{3\times6}{9}=2\ \mu\text{F} \), \( Q=2\times90=180\ \mu\text{C} \) on each.

\( V_3=\dfrac{180}{3}=60\ \text{V} \); the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage.
questions.hint: Same charge on both; V = Q/C.
distractor_logic: Swaps the voltages, as if V divided in proportion to C.
Splits the voltage equally.
Gives each capacitor the full supply voltage, as in parallel.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Capacitors of \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) are connected in parallel across a \( 12\ \text{V} \) battery. The charge on the \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is
questions.explanation:
In parallel both have 12 V.

\( Q_4=4\times12=48\ \mu\text{C} \).
questions.hint: Parallel: same voltage.
distractor_logic: Gives the charge on the 2 microfarad capacitor.
Gives the total charge of the combination.
Uses the series-combination charge, as if both carried a common charge.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) and a \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor are connected in parallel, and this pair is connected in series with a \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation:
Parallel pair: \( 2+4=6\ \mu\text{F} \).

In series with 3: \( \dfrac{6\times3}{6+3}=2\ \mu\text{F} \).
questions.hint: Reduce the parallel pair first.
distractor_logic: Adds all three as if in parallel.
Swaps the rules, using the resistor formulas: product-over-sum for the pair, then adding the 3.
Treats all three as in series.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: An \( 8\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor carries a charge of \( 40\ \mu\text{C} \). The energy stored is
distractor_logic: Forgets the factor one half.
Divides by 4C instead of 2C.
Multiplies Q by C instead of dividing Q squared by C.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Two identical capacitors are connected first in parallel and then in series, each time across the same voltage V. The ratio \( U_{\text{parallel}}:U_{\text{series}} \) of total stored energies is
questions.explanation:
Parallel: \( C_{eq}=2C \). Series: \( C_{eq}=C/2 \).

At the same V, \( U=\dfrac12C_{eq}V^2 \), so the ratio is \( 2C:\dfrac C2=4:1 \).
questions.hint: At fixed V, energy is proportional to \( C_{eq} \).
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio.
Compares with a single capacitor instead of the series pair.
Energy depends on the equivalent capacitance, which differs.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: The potential difference across a given capacitor is doubled. The energy stored becomes
questions.explanation: \( U=\dfrac12CV^2 \) with C unchanged, so doubling V multiplies U by 4.
questions.hint: Energy goes as V squared.
distractor_logic: Treats U as linear in V.
U depends on V.
U rises with V, not falls.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: The electric field in a region of air is \( 1\times10^{6}\ \text{V m}^{-1} \). Take \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2} \). The energy density in the field is about
questions.explanation:
\( u=\dfrac12\epsilon_0E^2=\dfrac12\times8.85\times10^{-12}\times10^{12} \).

\( u\approx4.43\ \text{J m}^{-3} \).
questions.hint: \( u=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \).
distractor_logic: Forgets the factor one half.
Forgets to square E.
Uses one quarter instead of one half.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Charges \( +3\ \text{nC} \), \( -4\ \text{nC} \) and \( +2\ \text{nC} \) are at distances \( 30\ \text{cm} \), \( 40\ \text{cm} \) and \( 50\ \text{cm} \) respectively from a point P, in different directions. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at P is
questions.explanation:
Contributions: \( \dfrac{9\times3}{0.3}=90\ \text{V} \), \( \dfrac{9\times(-4)}{0.4}=-90\ \text{V} \), \( \dfrac{9\times2}{0.5}=36\ \text{V} \).

Sum algebraically: \( 90-90+36=36\ \text{V} \). The directions do not matter for a scalar.
questions.hint: Find each signed contribution separately, then add.
distractor_logic: Adds all three magnitudes, ignoring the negative charge.
Reverses every sign.
Keeps only the nearest charge's contribution.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Charges \( q \) and \( 2q \) are at two vertices of an equilateral triangle. What charge \( Q \) must be placed at the third vertex so that the potential at the centroid is zero?
questions.explanation:
All vertices are the same distance \( r \) from the centroid, so \( V=\dfrac{k}{r}(q+2q+Q) \).

Setting \( V=0 \) gives \( Q=-3q \). No angles are involved because potential is a scalar.
questions.hint: Equal distances mean the charges themselves must sum to zero.
distractor_logic: Treats the contributions as vectors at \( 120^\circ \), finding a 'resultant' \( \sqrt3 q \) to cancel; that is a field-style calculation.
Gets the magnitude right but the wrong sign; a positive charge would increase V.
Cancels only the larger charge 2q, forgetting q.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A charge \( +4\ \mu\text{C} \) is at \( x=0 \) and \( -1\ \mu\text{C} \) is at \( x=0.3\ \text{m} \). At which points on the x-axis (other than infinity) is the electric potential zero?
questions.explanation:
Between the charges: \( \dfrac{4}{x}=\dfrac{1}{0.3-x}\Rightarrow x=0.24\ \text{m} \).

Beyond the negative charge: \( \dfrac{4}{x}=\dfrac{1}{x-0.3}\Rightarrow x=0.40\ \text{m} \).

To the left of the +4 charge, it is always closer and larger, so V cannot vanish there.
questions.hint: Check both between the charges and outside them, near the smaller one.
distractor_logic: Misses the second zero outside the charges, beyond the smaller charge.
Misses the zero between the charges.
Uses the field-zero condition \( 4/x^2=1/(x-0.3)^2 \); potential zeros use \( 1/r \).

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: The potential at a point on the axis of a short dipole, at distance \( r \) from its centre, is \( V_0 \). What is the potential at another point at the same distance \( r \), on a line making \( 120^\circ \) with the dipole axis?
questions.explanation:
\( V\propto\cos\theta \) at fixed \( r \), and \( V_0 \) corresponds to \( \cos0^\circ=1 \).

So \( V=V_0\cos120^\circ=-\dfrac{V_0}{2} \); the point is nearer the negative charge.
questions.hint: Keep the sign of \( \cos120^\circ \).
distractor_logic: Drops the sign of \( \cos120^\circ \).
Uses \( \sin120^\circ \) with a negative sign instead of \( \cos120^\circ \).
Uses \( \cos^2120^\circ \), which also loses the sign.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: For a short dipole, the potential at a point on its axis \( 2\ \text{m} \) from the centre is \( 20\ \text{V} \). The potential at a point \( 4\ \text{m} \) from the centre, on a line making \( 60^\circ \) with the axis, is
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2} \), so \( kp=20\times2^2=80\ \text{V m}^2 \).

At the new point: \( V=\dfrac{80\times\cos60^\circ}{4^2}=\dfrac{40}{16}=2.5\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Scale by \( \cos\theta \) and by \( 1/r^2 \).
distractor_logic: Applies the \( 1/r^2 \) scaling but drops \( \cos60^\circ \).
Scales with \( 1/r^3 \), as for the dipole field.
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) in place of \( \cos60^\circ \).

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: A total charge of \( 6\ \text{nC} \) is spread non-uniformly around a thin ring of radius \( 30\ \text{cm} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The potential at the centre of the ring is
options: It cannot be found without knowing the charge distribution
questions.explanation:
Every bit of charge \( dq \) is at the same distance \( R \) from the centre, so \( V=\sum\dfrac{k\,dq}{R}=\dfrac{kQ}{R} \), whatever the distribution.

\( V=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times6\times10^{-9}}{0.3}=180\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Potential adds as scalars, so only distances matter, not directions.
distractor_logic: Confuses potential with field; field contributions may cancel, but scalar potentials of like charges cannot.
The non-uniformity would affect the field at the centre, not the potential.
Divides by \( R^2 \), as for a field.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: In a region, the potential is \( V=2x^2+3y \) (V in volts, x and y in metres). The electric field at the point \( (1\ \text{m},\,2\ \text{m}) \) is
questions.explanation:
\( E_x=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}=-4x=-4 \) at \( x=1 \).

\( E_y=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}=-3 \), independent of y.

So \( \vec E=(-4\hat i-3\hat j)\ \text{V m}^{-1} \), magnitude \( 5\ \text{V m}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate with respect to each coordinate separately and apply the minus sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the minus sign, giving a field that points towards higher potential.
Differentiates \( 2x^2 \) as \( 2x \), missing the factor 2 from the power.
Substitutes y = 2 into \( 3y \) instead of differentiating it.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Around an isolated point charge, the \( 60\ \text{V} \) equipotential surface has radius \( 10\ \text{cm} \). The radius of the \( 20\ \text{V} \) equipotential surface is
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{kq}{r} \), so \( Vr \) is constant: \( 60\times10=20\times r \).

\( r=30\ \text{cm} \). Lower potential lies farther out, and the spacing widens as the field weakens.
questions.hint: For a point charge, \( V\propto1/r \).
distractor_logic: Makes r proportional to V instead of inversely proportional.
Uses \( r\propto1/\sqrt V \), as if V went like \( 1/r^2 \) (the field law).
Uses \( r\propto1/V^2 \).

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A particle with charge \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) is released from rest at a point where \( V=100\ \text{V} \) and moves, under electric forces alone, to a point where \( V=40\ \text{V} \). The change in its kinetic energy is
questions.explanation:
Energy conservation: \( \Delta K=-\Delta U=-q(V_B-V_A) \).

\( \Delta K=-2\times10^{-6}\times(40-100)=+1.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \). A positive charge speeds up as it moves to lower potential.
questions.hint: A free positive charge moves towards lower potential and speeds up.
distractor_logic: Gets the sign wrong; the field does positive work on a positive charge moving to lower V.
Adds the potentials instead of taking their difference.
Uses only \( qV_B \).

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: An electron is released from rest in a region where the potential increases steadily along +x. The electron
options: moves along -x, towards lower potential, and its potential energy decreases
moves along +x, towards higher potential, and its potential energy decreases
moves along +x, towards higher potential, and its potential energy increases
stays at rest, because it cannot move against the potential gradient
questions.explanation:
The field points towards decreasing V, i.e. along -x. The force on the negative electron is opposite to E, i.e. along +x.

Its potential energy \( U=qV=-eV \) decreases as V rises, while its kinetic energy grows.
questions.hint: Force on a negative charge is opposite to the field.
distractor_logic: Treats the electron like a positive charge.
Right direction, but \( U=-eV \) falls as V rises.
Any free charge in a nonzero field accelerates.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Points A and C lie on the same equipotential surface at \( 25\ \text{V} \); point B is at \( 75\ \text{V} \). A charge \( +4\ \mu\text{C} \) is carried slowly from A to B and then from B to C. The total work done by the external agent is
questions.explanation:
A to B: \( 4\times10^{-6}\times(75-25)=+2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \). B to C: \( 4\times10^{-6}\times(25-75)=-2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \).

Total \( =q(V_C-V_A)=0 \), since A and C are at the same potential.
questions.hint: Only the start and end points matter.
distractor_logic: Adds the size of both legs, ignoring that the second leg has negative work.
Counts only the A to B leg.
Counts only the B to C leg.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: A uniform field \( E=400\ \text{V m}^{-1} \) exists in a region. A charge \( +3\ \mu\text{C} \) is moved slowly through \( 0.5\ \text{m} \) along a line making \( 60^\circ \) with the field direction. The work done by the external agent is
questions.explanation:
\( V_B-V_A=-Ed\cos60^\circ=-400\times0.5\times\dfrac12=-100\ \text{V} \).

\( W=q(V_B-V_A)=3\times10^{-6}\times(-100)=-3\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \); the field does the work, the agent only holds back.
questions.hint: Moving with the field lowers the potential.
distractor_logic: Uses \( V_A-V_B \), flipping the sign.
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) instead of \( \cos60^\circ \).
Ignores the angle and uses the full 0.5 m along the field.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Charges \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \), \( -1\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \( 30\ \text{cm} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The total potential energy of the system is
questions.explanation:
Three pairs, all at 0.3 m. Sum of pair products (in \( \mu\text{C}^2 \)): \( (2)(-1)+(2)(1)+(-1)(1)=-1 \).

\( U=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times(-1\times10^{-12})}{0.3}=-0.03\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Add the three signed pair products.
distractor_logic: Uses magnitudes of all products, ignoring signs.
Double counts each pair.
Right magnitude, wrong sign.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Two charges, each \( +3\ \mu\text{C} \), are fixed at \( x=-0.3\ \text{m} \) and \( x=+0.3\ \text{m} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work needed to bring a charge \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) slowly from infinity to the origin is
questions.explanation:
At the origin the fields cancel, but potentials add: \( V=2\times\dfrac{9\times10^9\times3\times10^{-6}}{0.3}=1.8\times10^5\ \text{V} \).

\( W=qV=10^{-6}\times1.8\times10^{5}=0.18\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Zero field at a point does not mean zero potential there.
distractor_logic: Assumes zero field at the origin means zero work; work depends on potential, which is not zero.
Counts only one of the fixed charges.
Uses \( 1/r^2 \), a field-style formula, for each charge.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Two conducting spheres of radii \( 10\ \text{cm} \) and \( 20\ \text{cm} \), far apart, are connected by a thin wire and charged. The ratio of surface charge densities, \( \sigma_{\text{small}}:\sigma_{\text{large}} \), is
questions.explanation:
Connected conductors share one potential: \( \dfrac{kq_1}{r_1}=\dfrac{kq_2}{r_2}\Rightarrow q\propto r \).

\( \sigma=\dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2}\propto\dfrac{1}{r} \), so \( \sigma_1:\sigma_2=r_2:r_1=2:1 \).
questions.hint: Equal potentials first, then divide by area.
distractor_logic: This is the charge ratio, not the density ratio.
Uses \( \sigma\propto1/r^2 \), forgetting that q itself grows with r.
Assumes equal density, which would give unequal potentials.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A hollow conducting sphere of radius \( 20\ \text{cm} \) carries a charge \( 4\ \text{nC} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The electric field and potential at a point \( 10\ \text{cm} \) from its centre are
questions.explanation:
Inside, E = 0, so V does not change from its surface value.

\( V=\dfrac{kQ}{R}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-9}}{0.2}=180\ \text{V} \) throughout the inside.
questions.hint: \( E=-dV/dr=0 \) inside means V is constant.
distractor_logic: Confuses zero field with zero potential.
Uses the distance of the interior point instead of R.
Uses the surface field \( kQ/R^2 \) inside, where the field is zero.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: In a hydrogen atom, the electron and proton are about \( 0.53\times10^{-10}\ \text{m} \) apart. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). With \( e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C} \), the electrostatic potential energy of the system is about
questions.explanation:
\( U=\dfrac{k(-e)(e)}{r}=-\dfrac{9\times10^9\times(1.6\times10^{-19})^2}{0.53\times10^{-10}}\approx-4.35\times10^{-18}\ \text{J} \).

Dividing by \( 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{J/eV} \): \( U\approx-27.2\ \text{eV} \).
questions.hint: Opposite charges give negative potential energy.
distractor_logic: Ignores that the charges are opposite.
13.6 eV is the total (kinetic plus potential) energy magnitude, not the potential energy.
Doubles the correct value.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: A point charge \( +q \) is placed off-centre inside a cavity in an uncharged, isolated spherical conductor. The charge on the outer surface of the conductor is
options: \( +q \), crowded on the side nearest the point charge
zero, because the conductor is uncharged
questions.explanation:
The cavity wall carries \( -q \) (non-uniform), which together with \( +q \) produces zero field in the metal.
