The outer \( +q \) feels no field from inside, so it spreads uniformly over the sphere, as if the inner arrangement did not exist.
questions.hint: The metal shields the outer surface from what happens inside.
distractor_logic: Only the cavity-wall charge is non-uniform; the outer surface is shielded.
Wrong sign; the outer surface must carry +q for overall neutrality.
The conductor is neutral overall, but its outer surface is not.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: An air capacitor has plate separation \( 3\ \text{mm} \) and capacitance \( 12\ \text{pF} \). A dielectric slab of \( K=2 \) and thickness \( 2\ \text{mm} \) is placed between the plates. The new capacitance is
questions.explanation:
\( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{d-t+t/K} \), with \( d-t+\dfrac tK=1+\dfrac22=2\ \text{mm} \).

Since \( C_0=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{3\ \text{mm}}=12\ \text{pF} \), \( C=12\times\dfrac32=18\ \text{pF} \).
questions.hint: Only part of the gap is filled: the slab acts like a thinner air gap.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by K as if the slab filled the whole gap.
Ignores the slab.
Uses \( d-t+tK \) instead of \( d-t+t/K \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) parallel plate capacitor is charged to \( 50\ \text{V} \) and disconnected. Its plates are then pulled apart to twice the original separation. The new potential difference is
questions.explanation:
Isolated: \( Q=4\times50=200\ \mu\text{C} \) stays fixed. New \( C=2\ \mu\text{F} \).

\( V=\dfrac{200}{2}=100\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Fixed charge, smaller capacitance.
distractor_logic: Halves V, as if C had doubled.
Holds V fixed, true only when connected.
Treats C as varying with \( 1/d^2 \).

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A capacitor carrying a free charge of \( 60\ \mu\text{C} \) on each plate is completely filled with a dielectric of \( K=3 \). The magnitude of the induced (bound) charge on each face of the dielectric is
questions.explanation:
Net field is \( E_0/K \), so net charge seen \( =Q/K=20\ \mu\text{C} \).

Induced charge \( Q_b=Q-\dfrac QK=Q\left(1-\dfrac1K\right)=60\times\dfrac23=40\ \mu\text{C} \).
questions.hint: The bound charge cancels part of the free charge, leaving Q/K.
distractor_logic: Reports Q/K, the net charge, not the induced charge.
Multiplies by K.
Assumes total cancellation, which would make the field zero.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: A \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) air capacitor is connected to a \( 10\ \text{V} \) battery and a dielectric slab of \( K=4 \) is slid in to fill it. The battery is then disconnected and the slab is pulled out. The final potential difference across the capacitor is
questions.explanation:
With the battery: \( C=8\ \mu\text{F} \), \( Q=8\times10=80\ \mu\text{C} \).

Disconnected, Q = 80 \( \mu\text{C} \) stays. Removing the slab: \( C=2\ \mu\text{F} \), so \( V=\dfrac{80}{2}=40\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Track which quantity is fixed at each stage.
distractor_logic: Assumes V stays at the battery value after disconnection.
Divides by K instead of multiplying.
Multiplies by K twice.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: An air capacitor has capacitance \( 10\ \text{pF} \). Half of the plate area is filled with a dielectric of \( K_1=2 \) and the other half with \( K_2=4 \), each slab filling the full gap. The new capacitance is
questions.explanation:
Side-by-side slabs share the same plates and V: two capacitors in parallel, each of area A/2.

\( C=\dfrac{K_1C_0}{2}+\dfrac{K_2C_0}{2}=10+20=30\ \text{pF} \).
questions.hint: Side-by-side regions share the same voltage.
distractor_logic: Combines the halves in series; side-by-side regions are in parallel.
Forgets that each dielectric covers only half the area.
Multiplies the dielectric constants.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: An air capacitor has capacitance \( 10\ \text{pF} \). The gap is filled with two slabs stacked one above the other, each of half the gap thickness, with \( K_1=3 \) and \( K_2=6 \). The new capacitance is
questions.explanation:
Stacked layers carry the same charge: two capacitors in series, each of gap d/2, i.e. \( 2K_1C_0 \) and \( 2K_2C_0 \): 60 pF and 120 pF.

\( C=\dfrac{60\times120}{60+120}=40\ \text{pF} \).
questions.hint: Stacked layers are in series.
distractor_logic: Averages K as if the slabs were side by side (parallel).
Forgets that each layer has half the gap, which doubles its capacitance.
Adds the dielectric constants.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 100\ \text{V} \) and a \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 50\ \text{V} \) are disconnected from their supplies and then joined, positive plate to positive plate. The common potential is
questions.explanation:
Total charge is conserved: \( Q=2\times100+3\times50=350\ \mu\text{C} \). In parallel, \( C=5\ \mu\text{F} \).

\( V=\dfrac{350}{5}=70\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Conserve charge, not voltage.
distractor_logic: Averages the voltages, ignoring the different capacitances.
Subtracts the charges, as if unlike plates were joined.
Adds the voltages, as if the capacitors were in series.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor charged to \( 20\ \text{V} \) is connected across an identical uncharged \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor. The energy lost (as heat and radiation) in the process is
questions.explanation:
Initially \( U_i=\dfrac12\times4\times10^{-6}\times20^2=8\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \). Charge 80 \( \mu\text{C} \) spreads over 8 \( \mu\text{F} \): V = 10 V.

\( U_f=\dfrac12\times8\times10^{-6}\times10^2=4\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \), so \( 4\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \) is lost: half the original energy.
questions.hint: Charge is conserved; energy is not.
distractor_logic: Assumes energy is conserved when charge redistributes.
Assumes all the original energy is lost.
Reports the final energy on one capacitor, not the loss.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is connected in series with a parallel combination of \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \), across an \( 18\ \text{V} \) battery. The charge on the \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is
questions.explanation:
Parallel pair = 6 \( \mu\text{F} \); with 3 in series, \( C_{eq}=2\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( Q=36\ \mu\text{C} \).

Voltage across the pair \( =\dfrac{36}{6}=6\ \text{V} \), so \( Q_4=4\times6=24\ \mu\text{C} \).
questions.hint: The series charge splits between the parallel capacitors.
distractor_logic: Gives the whole series charge to the 4 microfarad capacitor; in parallel the charge divides.
Gives the charge on the 2 microfarad capacitor.
Puts the full battery voltage across the 4 microfarad capacitor.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Capacitors of \( 3\ \mu\text{F} \) and \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) are connected in series across a \( 90\ \text{V} \) supply. The energy stored in the \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is
questions.explanation:
\( Q=C_{eq}V=2\times90=180\ \mu\text{C} \), so \( V_6=\dfrac{180}{6}=30\ \text{V} \).

\( U_6=\dfrac12\times6\times10^{-6}\times30^2=2.7\times10^{-3}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Find its own voltage first.
distractor_logic: Gives the energy in the 3 microfarad capacitor.
Applies the full 90 V across the 6 microfarad capacitor.
Gives the total energy of the combination.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A capacitor stores \( 0.02\ \text{J} \) of energy when charged to \( 200\ \text{V} \). Its capacitance is
questions.explanation:
\( U=\dfrac12CV^2\Rightarrow C=\dfrac{2U}{V^2}=\dfrac{0.04}{40000} \).

\( C=1\times10^{-6}\ \text{F}=1\ \mu\text{F} \).
questions.hint: Rearrange \( U=\tfrac12CV^2 \).
distractor_logic: Drops the factor 2 when rearranging.
Divides by V instead of V squared.
Drops the factor 2 and divides by V instead of V squared.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Identical capacitors of \( 1\ \mu\text{F} \) each can safely withstand at most \( 400\ \text{V} \). What is the minimum number needed to build a \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) combination that can be used across \( 1000\ \text{V} \)?
questions.explanation:
Series rows share the voltage: need \( 400n\ge1000 \), so n = 3 per row, giving \( \dfrac13\ \mu\text{F} \) per row.

Parallel rows add: m rows give \( \dfrac m3=2 \), so m = 6. Total \( 3\times6=18 \).
questions.hint: Series for voltage, parallel for capacitance.
distractor_logic: Counts only the rows.
Counts only the capacitors in one row.
Uses 2 per row (rounding 2.5 down), which would overload each capacitor.

questions.question: Three charges, each \( +2\ \text{nC} \), sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, each \( 30\ \text{cm} \) from the centroid. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work needed to bring a \( +5\ \mu\text{C} \) charge slowly from infinity to the centroid is
questions.explanation:
Potential at the centroid (scalar sum): \( V=3\times\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-9}}{0.3}=180\ \text{V} \).

\( W=qV=5\times10^{-6}\times180=9\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: The field at the centroid is zero, but the potential is not.
distractor_logic: Uses zero field at the centroid to conclude zero work; work depends on potential.
Includes only one of the three charges.
Wrong sign; pushing a positive charge towards positive charges needs positive work.

questions.question: At a point near an isolated point charge, the potential is \( 600\ \text{V} \) and the field magnitude is \( 200\ \text{V m}^{-1} \). The distance of the point from the charge is
questions.explanation:
For a point charge, \( V=\dfrac{kq}{r} \) and \( E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2} \), so \( \dfrac VE=r \).

\( r=\dfrac{600}{200}=3\ \text{m} \) (and \( q=\dfrac{Vr}{k}=2\times10^{-7}\ \text{C} \)).
questions.hint: Divide V by E for a point charge.

Takes the square root of V/E, as if V went like 1/r squared.
Squares V/E.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor has \( 100\ \text{V} \) across plates \( 2\ \text{mm} \) apart. The work done by an external agent in slowly carrying a \( +3\ \mu\text{C} \) charge from the negative plate to the positive plate is
questions.explanation:
\( W=q(V_+-V_-)=3\times10^{-6}\times100 \).

\( W=3\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \), positive because a positive charge is pushed to higher potential. The gap width does not enter.
questions.hint: Use \( W=q(V_B-V_A) \) between the plates.
distractor_logic: Uses \( V_A-V_B \), the wrong order.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: An isolated air capacitor has a field of \( 3\times10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1} \) between its plates, which are \( 2\ \text{mm} \) apart. A dielectric slab of \( K=3 \) is inserted to fill the gap. The new potential difference is
questions.explanation:
Isolated: charge fixed, so the field drops by K: \( E=\dfrac{3\times10^5}{3}=1\times10^5\ \text{V m}^{-1} \).

\( V=Ed=10^5\times2\times10^{-3}=200\ \text{V} \).
questions.hint: Find the new field, then use \( V=Ed \).
distractor_logic: Uses the original field, as if V stayed fixed.
Multiplies the field by K.
Divides by K twice.

questions.topic: Capacitors, Capacitance, and Parallel Plate Capacitors with Dielectrics
questions.question: The plates of an isolated parallel plate capacitor carry surface charge densities \( +8.85\times10^{-7}\ \text{C m}^{-2} \) and \( -8.85\times10^{-7}\ \text{C m}^{-2} \). Take \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2} \). The fields between the plates and outside them are
questions.explanation:
Each plate alone gives \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0=5\times10^4\ \text{V m}^{-1} \). Between the plates these add; outside they cancel.

So \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0=1\times10^5\ \text{V m}^{-1} \) between and zero outside, matching the conductor-surface result \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: Superpose the two plates' fields in each region.
distractor_logic: Uses a single plate's field in both regions.
Outside, the two plates' fields cancel.
Uses \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) between the plates, forgetting the second plate.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 6\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 20\ \text{V} \) and disconnected from the battery. A dielectric of \( K=3 \) is then inserted to fill the gap. The energy now stored is
questions.explanation:
Initially \( U_0=\dfrac12\times6\times10^{-6}\times20^2=1.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{J} \).

Q is fixed and C triples, so \( U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{U_0}{3}=4\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Isolated: use the form of U that has Q in it.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by K, using the fixed-voltage rule while the capacitor is isolated.
Assumes stored energy is unchanged.
Divides by K twice.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor remains connected to a \( 50\ \text{V} \) battery while a dielectric of \( K=4 \) is inserted to fill the gap. The energy stored becomes
questions.explanation:
Initially \( U_0=\dfrac12\times2\times10^{-6}\times50^2=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{J} \).

V fixed and C becomes \( 8\ \mu\text{F} \): \( U=\dfrac12CV^2=4U_0=1\times10^{-2}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Connected: use the form of U that has V in it.
distractor_logic: Divides by K, using the fixed-charge rule while still connected.
Assumes stored energy is unchanged.
Multiplies by K twice.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: Two \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) air capacitors are in series across a \( 12\ \text{V} \) battery. With the battery connected, a dielectric of \( K=3 \) is inserted to fill one of them. The potential difference across the filled capacitor becomes
questions.explanation:
Now \( C_1=12\ \mu\text{F} \), \( C_2=4\ \mu\text{F} \): \( C_{eq}=\dfrac{12\times4}{16}=3\ \mu\text{F} \), \( Q=36\ \mu\text{C} \) on each.

\( V_1=\dfrac{36}{12}=3\ \text{V} \) (and 9 V across the other).
questions.hint: Series capacitors share one charge; recompute it after the change.
distractor_logic: Assumes the voltage split is unchanged.
Gives the voltage across the unfilled capacitor.
Divides the old 6 V by K, treating the capacitor as isolated.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: An air capacitor of \( 10\ \text{pF} \) has half of its plate area filled (across the full gap) with a dielectric of \( K=5 \). It is charged to \( 100\ \text{V} \). The energy stored is
questions.explanation:
The two halves act in parallel: \( C=\dfrac{10}{2}+\dfrac{5\times10}{2}=30\ \text{pF} \).

\( U=\dfrac12CV^2=\dfrac12\times30\times10^{-12}\times10^4=1.5\times10^{-7}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Side-by-side halves are in parallel.
distractor_logic: Ignores the dielectric.
Applies K to the whole capacitor.
Combines the halves in series.

questions.topic: Electric Potential: Due to a Point Charge, System of Charges, and an Electric Dipole
questions.question: Two equal charges \( +q \) are separated by \( 2a \). At the midpoint between them, the magnitudes of the electric field E and potential V are
questions.explanation:
Fields are vectors: equal and opposite at the midpoint, so E = 0.

Potentials are scalars of the same sign: \( V=\dfrac{kq}{a}+\dfrac{kq}{a}=\dfrac{2kq}{a} \). Zero field only means V has zero slope there, not zero value.
questions.hint: Vectors can cancel; positive scalars cannot.
distractor_logic: Assumes zero field implies zero potential.
Swaps the roles: it is the fields that cancel, not the potentials.
Adds the fields as if they pointed the same way.

questions.question: A charge is carried from a distant point to a point close to a short dipole, moving only along the dipole's equatorial line. The work done by the external agent is
options: positive or negative depending on how close it gets
questions.explanation:
Every equatorial point is equidistant from \( +q \) and \( -q \), so V = 0 all along it: the equatorial plane is an equipotential.

\( W=q(V_B-V_A)=q(0-0)=0 \), even though the field there is not zero.
questions.hint: What is the potential everywhere on the equatorial line?
distractor_logic: Assumes a nonzero field forces nonzero work; motion along an equipotential needs none.
Same error with the opposite sign.

questions.question: Electric field lines always meet the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium at right angles because
options: the charge density is uniform over every conductor surface
the surface is an equipotential, and the field is always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces
the field inside the conductor is maximum at the surface
field lines are repelled by the free electrons
questions.explanation:
A tangential field component would push charges along the surface, so in equilibrium it must vanish: the surface is an equipotential.

Field lines are normal to equipotentials, hence normal to the conductor surface.
questions.hint: Link equilibrium, equipotential and field direction.
distractor_logic: Density varies with curvature; the right-angle rule holds regardless.
The field inside is zero everywhere, including just inside the surface.
This is not the reason; the geometry follows from the equipotential condition.

questions.question: A \( 5\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged fully by a \( 12\ \text{V} \) battery. The work done by the battery and the energy finally stored in the capacitor are, respectively,
questions.explanation:
The battery moves \( Q=CV=60\ \mu\text{C} \) through a fixed 12 V: \( W=QV=7.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \).

The capacitor's voltage rises from 0 to 12 V, so it stores \( \dfrac12QV=3.6\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \); the other half is lost in the connecting wires.

questions.question: Charges \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) are fixed at two vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \( 20\ \text{cm} \). Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work needed to bring a \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) charge from infinity to the third vertex is
questions.explanation:
Potential at the third vertex: \( V=2\times\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-6}}{0.2}=1.8\times10^5\ \text{V} \).

\( W=qV=10^{-6}\times1.8\times10^5=0.18\ \text{J} \). The existing pair's energy was already stored before this step.
questions.hint: Only the two new pairs formed by the moving charge count.
distractor_logic: Adds the energy of the fixed pair, which is not part of this step.
Counts only one of the fixed charges.
Combines the two contributions as vectors at \( 60^\circ \); potential terms add as scalars.

questions.question: A \( 4\ \mu\text{F} \) parallel plate capacitor is charged to \( 50\ \text{V} \) and disconnected. Its plate separation is then doubled. The energy stored becomes
questions.explanation:
\( Q=200\ \mu\text{C} \) stays fixed; C becomes \( 2\ \mu\text{F} \).

\( U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{(200\times10^{-6})^2}{4\times10^{-6}}=1\times10^{-2}\ \text{J} \), double the original; the extra is work done pulling the plates apart.
questions.hint: Isolated: Q fixed, so use Q squared over 2C.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \tfrac12CV^2 \) with V held fixed, which applies only when connected.
Assumes energy stays the same.
Quadruples instead of doubling.

questions.question: An air capacitor with plate separation \( 3\ \text{mm} \) has capacitance \( 6\ \text{pF} \). An uncharged metal slab of thickness \( 1\ \text{mm} \) is inserted parallel to the plates. The new capacitance is
questions.explanation:
The field inside the metal is zero, so the potential drop occurs only across the remaining \( 3-1=2\ \text{mm} \) of air.

\( C=\dfrac{\epsilon_0A}{2\ \text{mm}}=6\times\dfrac32=9\ \text{pF} \).
questions.hint: No field inside the metal: it simply shortens the air gap.
distractor_logic: Adds the slab thickness to the gap instead of subtracting it.
Assumes a metal slab has no effect.
Only a slab filling the whole gap would short the plates.

questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges and Electrostatics of Conductors
questions.question: Inside a charged hollow conducting sphere, the potential V and field E behave as follows:
options: V is constant and equal to its surface value, and E = 0
V is constant and E is nonzero
V decreases towards the centre and E is nonzero
questions.explanation:
Charge on a conductor sits on its outer surface, and E = 0 inside.

Since \( E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0 \), V cannot change inside: it stays at the surface value \( kQ/R \).
questions.hint: A zero gradient means a constant value.
distractor_logic: Confuses zero field with zero potential.
A constant V means zero gradient, so E must be zero.
There is no field inside to cause any change in V.

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Near an isolated negative point charge, as you move directly away from the charge, the potential
options: decreases (becomes more negative), and the field points away from the charge
increases, and the field points away from the charge
increases (becomes less negative), and the field points back towards the charge
stays constant, since the charge is negative
questions.explanation:
\( V=\dfrac{k(-q)}{r} \) is negative and rises towards 0 as r increases.

The field points towards decreasing potential, i.e. back towards the charge, consistent with field lines ending on a negative charge.
questions.hint: Field points from higher to lower potential.
distractor_logic: Reverses both the trend of V and the field direction.
Right about V, but the field must point towards lower V, which is towards the charge.
V depends on r, whatever the sign of the charge.

questions.question: A short dipole of moment \( 4\times10^{-9}\ \text{C m} \) is placed in a uniform field of \( 5\times10^{4}\ \text{N C}^{-1} \) with its moment at \( 60^\circ \) to the field. Its potential energy is
questions.explanation:
\( U=-pE\cos\theta=-(4\times10^{-9})(5\times10^4)\cos60^\circ \).

\( U=-2\times10^{-4}\times\dfrac12=-1\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \); it is lowest when p is along E.
questions.hint: \( U=-\vec p\cdot\vec E \).
distractor_logic: Drops the minus sign.
Uses \( \sin\theta \), which belongs in the torque, not the energy.
Ignores \( \cos\theta \).

questions.topic: Equipotential Surfaces and the Relationship Between Electric Field and Potential
questions.question: Two equal positive point charges are some distance apart. Their equipotential surfaces are
options: nearly spherical around each charge close to it, and nearly spherical around the midpoint far away from both
parallel planes perpendicular to the line joining them
a single set of spheres centred on the midpoint at all distances
spheres centred on each charge, unchanged at all distances
questions.explanation:
Very close to one charge its own potential dominates, so surfaces are small spheres around it.

Far away the pair looks like a single charge 2q at the midpoint, so surfaces become large spheres around the midpoint. In between they merge, since potentials add as scalars.
questions.hint: Think near one charge, then very far from both.
distractor_logic: Planes belong to a uniform field.
Close to one charge, its own potential dominates.
Far away the two contributions merge into one effective charge.

questions.question: Two identical isolated conducting spheres of radius \( 9\ \text{cm} \) (capacitance \( 10\ \text{pF} \) each) are far apart. One is at \( 1000\ \text{V} \) and the other is uncharged. They are connected by a thin wire. The energy lost in the process is
questions.explanation:
Initial: \( Q=10\ \text{pF}\times1000=10\ \text{nC} \), \( U_i=\dfrac12\times10^{-11}\times10^6=5\times10^{-6}\ \text{J} \).

Equal spheres share charge equally: V = 500 V, \( U_f=\dfrac12\times2\times10^{-11}\times500^2=2.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{J} \). Loss \( =2.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Charge is conserved as the conductors reach a common potential; energy is not.
distractor_logic: Assumes energy is conserved in charge sharing.
Reports the initial energy as the loss.
Reports the energy on one sphere after sharing.

questions.question: An electron is released from rest near the negative plate of a capacitor whose plates differ in potential by \( 100\ \text{V} \). Using \( e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C} \), the electron
options: moves towards the negative plate and gains \( 1.6\times10^{-17}\ \text{J} \) of kinetic energy
moves towards the positive plate and gains \( 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} \) of kinetic energy
moves towards the positive plate and gains \( 1.6\times10^{-17}\ \text{J} \) of kinetic energy
moves towards the positive plate and loses \( 1.6\times10^{-17}\ \text{J} \) of kinetic energy
questions.explanation:
A negative charge is pushed opposite to E, i.e. towards higher potential (the positive plate).

\( \Delta K=-q\Delta V=-(-1.6\times10^{-19})(100)=1.6\times10^{-17}\ \text{J} \) = 100 eV.
questions.hint: Negative charges move towards higher potential.
distractor_logic: Treats the electron like a positive charge.
Uses 1 V instead of 100 V.
Gets the direction right but the energy change backwards.

E = V/d must double when V doubles and d is fixed.

questions.question: An isolated charged parallel plate capacitor has its plate separation doubled. Using the idea of energy density, the stored energy doubles because
options: \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0 \) is unchanged (fixed charge), so the energy density is unchanged while the volume of field doubles
the field doubles, so the energy density doubles while the volume is unchanged
the field halves, so energy density falls but the volume quadruples
the charge doubles, so \( U=Q^2/2C \) doubles
questions.explanation:
The plates' charge, and hence \( \sigma \), stay fixed, so \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0 \) and \( u=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \) are unchanged.

The field now fills twice the volume Ad, so the energy doubles.
questions.hint: What sets the field between the plates of an isolated capacitor?
distractor_logic: The field depends on sigma, not on the separation.
Neither the field nor the volume change like this.
The charge on an isolated capacitor cannot change.

questions.explanation:
At the surface \( V=\dfrac{kQ}{R} \) and \( E=\dfrac{kQ}{R^2} \), so \( E=\dfrac VR \).

\( E=\dfrac{900}{0.1}=9000\ \text{V m}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Relate E and V at the surface of a sphere.
distractor_logic: Multiplies V by R.
Takes the potential value as the field.
Zero is the field inside, not just outside.

questions.question: A thin ring of radius \( 30\ \text{cm} \) carries \( +6\ \text{nC} \) uniformly. A \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) charge at its centre is moved slowly to infinity. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The work done by the external agent is
questions.explanation:
\( V_{\text{centre}}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times6\times10^{-9}}{0.3}=180\ \text{V} \), \( V_\infty=0 \).

\( W=q(V_\infty-V_{\text{centre}})=2\times10^{-6}\times(0-180)=-3.6\times10^{-4}\ \text{J} \); repulsion does the work.
questions.hint: Use \( W=q(V_{\text{final}}-V_{\text{initial}}) \).
distractor_logic: Uses the reversed order of potentials.
Uses zero field at the centre to conclude zero work.
Uses \( kQ/R^2 \), a field-style expression, for V.

questions.question: A very thin uncharged metal sheet is slid into a charged parallel plate capacitor, parallel to and midway between the plates. The capacitance
questions.explanation:
Induced charges appear on the two faces of the sheet, but the field between the plates is unchanged in the gaps and zero only inside the negligible thickness of metal.

The total potential difference is unchanged, so C = Q/V is unchanged (two d/2 gaps in series give the original C).
questions.hint: A slab of zero thickness removes no air gap.
distractor_logic: The sheet removes no gap width.
Two half-gaps in series combine back to the original capacitance.
The sheet is insulated from both plates, so it does not short them.

Uses only \( qV_B \), as if starting from infinity.

questions.topic: Combination of Capacitors and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
questions.question: A dielectric slab is brought near the edge of an isolated charged capacitor and is drawn into the gap. During this process,
options: the stored energy increases, supplied by the work done by the field
the stored energy stays constant, because the capacitor is isolated
the stored energy decreases, and an external agent must push the slab in
the stored energy decreases, and the field does positive work pulling the slab in
questions.explanation:
Isolated: Q fixed, C rises, so \( U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C} \) falls.

The lost energy appears as work done by the fringing field pulling the slab in; the slab is attracted, not repelled.
questions.hint: Isolated capacitor: which form of U applies?
distractor_logic: Energy increases only if the battery stays connected.
Being isolated fixes Q, not U.
The slab is pulled in; an agent would have to hold it back, not push.

questions.question: Charges \( +2\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( -2\ \mu\text{C} \) are \( 20\ \text{cm} \) apart. A third charge \( +1\ \mu\text{C} \) is brought from infinity to a point on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Take \( k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2} \). The total potential energy of the three-charge system is
questions.explanation:
The bisector is an equipotential at V = 0, so the third charge's two pair terms cancel: \( \dfrac{kq_3(+2)}{r}+\dfrac{kq_3(-2)}{r}=0 \).

Only the original pair remains: \( U=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times(2)(-2)\times10^{-12}}{0.2}=-0.18\ \text{J} \).
questions.hint: Three pairs; two of them cancel on the bisector.
distractor_logic: Assumes the whole system has zero energy because the third charge sits at V = 0; the original pair still has energy.
Drops the sign of the unlike pair.
Halves the pair energy.
